state.question:
Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, parallel gripper, about 15 N available at the flange), SO-101 leader/follower arms for teleoperation and imitation learning, Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags and 3D-printed fixtures. Our alloy program (FLAIME) is an AI-guided closed loop for aluminium alloys made by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF): CALPHAD screening and cost-aware Bayesian optimization choose compositions; charges of 250 to 300 g (machined 6063 cups with press-fit plugs, or bar slugs and master-alloy pieces) are atomized in an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer; then the powder is collected, weighed in six size fractions, sieved, split, jarred and labelled, sampled and sealed for oxygen analysis, tested for flowability, and mounted on SEM pin stubs (seven or eight per run) for morphology and EDS; printed specimens (single tracks, density cubes, ASTM E8 sub-size tensile bars) go to Archimedes density, Vickers hardness, metallography and tensile testing. Our own schedule estimates 10 to 15 person-hours of hands-on work per atomizer run, mostly after the run, and none of it is timed yet. Aluminium powder is a combustible metal (NFPA 484, now NFPA 660); operators wear full-face respirators for open-powder work; and the arm will stay out of the atomizer chamber. Peer efforts we know of include CMU's Materials Innovation Cloud Lab (also a rePOWDER), Texas A&M's metals self-driving lab, robotic metallography efforts, and printer-based SEM powder preparation (Milsted et al. 2025, EMSBot).

Question. What is the state of the art (2015 to 2026) in automating the hands-on steps of powder-metallurgy and additive-manufacturing alloy-development loops, and which steps have measured results?
(1) Post-atomization powder workup: powder collection, sieving and classification (loading sieve shakers), riffling or splitting, mass balance, jarring and labelling, and sealing samples for O/N/H analysis. Which have been automated with arms or other equipment, with what throughput, success rate, recovery and cross-contamination control between alloys?
(2) Powder characterization sample preparation: dispersing powder onto SEM stubs, automated SEM imaging and particle-shape analysis, sample introduction for laser-diffraction particle sizing, and automated flowability, apparent and tap density measurements.
(3) Solid-specimen steps: removing parts from LPBF build plates, sectioning, mounting, grinding and polishing (robotic metallography), automated Archimedes density, automated Vickers or micro-hardness, and robotic loading of tensile specimens. Give reported success rates, cycle times and failure modes.
(4) Charge preparation: robotic weighing and kitting of alloy charges from pieces or powders, and crucible loading.
(5) Safety: what NFPA 484/660, ATEX or published guidance requires of robots and electronics that handle open or closed combustible metal powders (ignition sources, grounding, dust-tight enclosures, inerting), any incident reports, and how autonomous metal-powder labs (including A-Lab follow-ups under inert atmosphere) handle this.
(6) Published time-per-sample or person-hour breakdowns for powder-metallurgy or AM alloy development that show where human hands dominate, to check our estimate that post-run workup is the bottleneck.
(7) For each step, judge whether it is realistically within reach of a 1.5 kg payload, low-force arm with a parallel gripper and Raspberry Pi cameras, or needs industrial equipment (for example press forces above a tonne).

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints and conference abstracts. For each claim give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

## State of the Art in Automating Hands-On Steps of Powder-Metallurgy and Additive-Manufacturing Alloy-Development Loops (2015–2026)

This review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature (2015–2026) on the automation of each hands-on step in powder-metallurgy and AM alloy-development workflows. For each step, we report what has been demonstrated with measured results, explicitly flag publication gaps, and assess feasibility for a 1.5 kg payload, low-force arm such as the AgileX PiPER.

The following table provides a step-by-step evidence map with citations, measured results, identified gaps, and feasibility assessment:

| Step | Published automation (system, reference, year) | Measured results | Gaps / limitations | Feasibility for 1.5 kg, low-force parallel-gripper arm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Post-atomization — collect powder from atomizer** | No peer-reviewed arm-based implementation located for rePOWDER or comparable small metal-atomizer collection. Published work discusses powder recycling and sieving, not autonomous collection. | **No published throughput, success, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Powder adhesion, inaccessible collector geometry, spills, airborne combustible dust, and alloy-to-alloy cleaning remain unquantified. | **Conditional.** The arm can move a sealed collector under 1.5 kg; open pouring should instead occur in a purpose-built grounded, contained transfer station. Do not place the arm in the atomizer chamber. |
| **1. Post-atomization — load/unload sieve stack; classify six fractions** | Commercial sieve shakers automate vibration, but no peer-reviewed robotic loading/unloading workflow with alloy-development metrics was located. Von Rohr notes that automated grinding and sieving have partially available commercial solutions requiring adaptation (rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 5-6). | **No published robotic success rate, recovery, cycle time, or cross-alloy carryover result found.** | A six-sieve stack plus 250–300 g powder may exceed payload; lids and pans can jam; retained powder adheres to mesh; cleaning and carryover dominate validation. | **Partial.** Arm can handle individual lightweight sieves, lids, and jars with fixtures; use a powered lift/clamp and stationary shaker for an assembled stack. |
| **1. Post-atomization — riffle/split powder** | No peer-reviewed robotic riffler or rotary splitter integrated into an AM-alloy loop was located. | **No published splitting precision, recovery, or contamination result found.** | Representative sampling requires controlled feed rate and validated increment geometry; cleaning inaccessible chutes between alloys is difficult. | **Reachable with dedicated equipment.** Arm can load a sealed rotary splitter or actuate indexed containers; freehand pouring is unlikely to be sufficiently repeatable. |
| **1. Post-atomization — mass balance of fractions** | Analytical balances and robot transport are mature; A-Lab and AlloyBot demonstrate robot-to-balance workflows, although not atomized-powder mass balance (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 4-7, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 7-7). | AlloyBot weighing is typically under 0.5 h per multielement charge; steady-state synthesis is about one alloy h⁻¹ (boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 30-35). **No powder-recovery validation reported.** | Static charge, powder on vessel exteriors, drafts, balance settling, and tare/container identity must be controlled. | **High.** Use capped standardized cups, balance-door automation, AprilTag/2D-code identity, and repeated gross/tare measurements. |
| **1. Post-atomization — jar, cap, label, and inventory fractions** | No peer-reviewed implementation located for robotic jarring and labelling of combustible AM metal powders. General autonomous labs demonstrate vial/rack transport (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 7-7, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 8-12). | **No published success, throughput, recovery, or cross-contamination metrics found.** | Screw-cap torque, liner seating, label adhesion, powder on threads, and identity reconciliation require validation. | **High for sealed jars.** Use keyed nests, low-torque caps or preassembled septum lids, barcode printing, and machine-readable verification; avoid manipulating loose powder directly. |
| **1. Post-atomization — prepare and seal O/N/H aliquots** | No peer-reviewed robotic workflow located for weighing and hermetically sealing metal-powder aliquots for inert-gas-fusion O/N/H analysis. | **No published cycle time, seal-failure rate, blank, or cross-contamination result found.** | Tiny aliquots, static, capsule folding/crimping, contamination blanks, and chain of custody are unresolved. | **Dispensing is conditional; sealing generally needs dedicated tooling.** Use a grounded enclosed dispenser plus pneumatic/electric crimper; the arm can transport capsules and sealed vials. |
| **2. Characterization — disperse powder onto SEM stub** | **EMSBot**, Milsted et al. 2025: modified 3D printer, vacuum pickup, carbon-tape stubs, and electrostatic deposition (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 2-3, milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 1-2). | Demonstrated at 10 kV, 10 mA, 5 s exposure; pickup is retried three times before requesting a human. Dispersion was more uniform and less agglomerated than manual preparation, but no aggregate throughput or success percentage was reported (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 3-5, milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 5-6). | High voltage and airborne-particle containment require redesign for combustible aluminium; deposition is particle-size selective and chemistry dependent. | **High for stub logistics; do not copy open electrostatic deposition for Al without a formal ignition-risk review.** A grounded, enclosed mechanical/vacuum dispersion module is preferable. |
| **2. Characterization — automated SEM imaging and particle-shape analysis** | DeCost et al. 2016 established autonomous computer-vision characterization; Bakas et al. 2022 reported Mask R-CNN powder segmentation. **AutoEMX/AutoEMXSp**, Giunto et al. 2025–2026, automates particle localization, EDS spots, spectral filtering, and phase clustering (giunto2025harnessingautomatedsemeds pages 1-4, giunto2026accuratesemedsquantification pages 3-5). | AutoEMX typically acquires about 100 spectra in 20–45 min per sample, processes tens of samples per day, and achieved compositions generally within 5–10% relative deviation across 74 samples and 38 elements (giunto2025harnessingautomatedsemeds pages 4-6, giunto2026accuratesemedsquantification pages 14-15, giunto2026accuratesemedsquantification pages 15-17). | Requires instrument API access and good dispersion; particles below roughly 2 µm are disfavoured; irregular geometry and substrate contamination still cause rejected spectra. | **High for stub exchange if the SEM has an automatable load lock; analysis is software-side.** Payload is not limiting. |
| **2. Characterization — introduce sample to laser-diffraction particle sizer** | Autosamplers and wet-dispersion units exist commercially, but no peer-reviewed arm-integrated metal-alloy workflow with recovery or carryover metrics was located. | **No relevant published robotic success rate or cycle time found.** | Representative subsampling, wet versus dry dispersion, ultrasound-induced deagglomeration, solvent compatibility, and complete line cleaning can bias PSD results. | **High for sealed-vial loading.** Use the instrument’s enclosed autosampler; avoid arm-based open pouring or aerosol-generating dry feed. |
| **2. Characterization — Hall/Carney flowability** | Published studies compare standardized manual funnels and automated rheometers; they do not report autonomous sample loading and cleaning. | No robotic metric found. Test results are method- and powder-dependent; standardized funnel tests can fail to flow for cohesive powders. | Start detection, funnel blockage, complete recovery, cleaning, humidity, and operator tapping strongly affect results. | **Moderate.** Arm can place a cup and actuate a gate; funnel filling, levelling, recovery, and cleaning should be enclosed and fixture-driven. |
| **2. Characterization — apparent and tap density** | Commercial tap-density instruments automate tapping/counting, but no peer-reviewed end-to-end robotic AM-powder workflow was located. | **No published robotic cycle time, success rate, or cross-contamination result found.** | Standardized filling, avoiding pre-compaction, reading volume, cleaning cylinders, and powder recovery remain manual. | **High for instrument tending.** Use lightweight keyed cylinders, machine vision for meniscus/bed height, and sealed transfer fixtures. |
| **3. Solid specimens — remove LPBF parts from build plate** | Industrial bandsaw, wire-EDM, and robotic machining cells automate removal, but no alloy-discovery-loop paper with general success and cycle metrics was located. | **No transferable success rate or cycle-time evidence found.** | Cutting loads, heat, swarf, supports, geometry variation, plate mass, and collision risk exceed benchtop-arm capabilities. | **Industrial equipment required.** The PiPER may tend small loose coupons after separation, not perform sawing, EDM, or high-force support removal. |
| **3. Solid specimens — section specimens** | Automated abrasive saws are commercially mature, but published closed-loop robotic loading metrics for AM alloy campaigns were not located. | **No relevant success-rate or cycle-time dataset found.** | Cutting force, coolant, guarding, clamping, blade wear, and geometry-specific fixturing dominate. | **Arm tending only.** A guarded automatic saw with pneumatic vise is required; robot should handle only lightweight, pre-fixtured samples. |
| **3. Solid specimens — hot/compression mounting** | Automated mounting presses exist commercially; no peer-reviewed robot-integrated AM-alloy workflow with measured reliability was located. | **No published robotic metric found.** | Typical mounting forces and temperatures are far beyond the arm; resin dosing and mould cleaning add contamination risks. | **Industrial press required.** Arm can load moulds/coupons using fixtures but cannot supply pressing force; cold-mount dispensing is more accessible. |
| **3. Solid specimens — grind, polish, clean, etch, and image** | **RASI**, BAM: UR5e, modified Qpol250 BOT, cleaning/etching station, and automated microscope; Lemiasheuski et al. 2023 and Moschetti et al. 2025 (moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 3-4, lemiasheuski2023developmentofan pages 7-10). | Up to 150 slices per specimen per day; largely unattended 24/7 operation; samples to about 15 × 15 × 15 mm³; z spacing to about 0.17 µm. Position variation is submicrometre laterally and below 1° rotationally (moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 4-4, moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 4-5). | Throughput decreases with extensive polishing, etching, or imaging; requires dedicated grinder/polisher, kinematic holders, fluid handling, and substantial integration. | **Transport feasible; polishing force is not.** PiPER can shuttle standardized pucks, but the grinder/polisher must clamp and apply load independently. |
| **3. Solid specimens — Vickers/microhardness** | Commercial automatic stages perform autofocus, indentation arrays, and image measurement; no peer-reviewed arm-loaded AM-alloy loop with reliability metrics was located. | **No published end-to-end loading success or cycle time found.** | Surface finish, focus, edge spacing, indentation recognition, and specimen tilt dominate error. | **High for puck loading** if the tester has an automatic stage and repeatable nest; the indenter supplies force. |
| **3. Solid specimens — Archimedes density** | No peer-reviewed robotic air/weighed-liquid density workflow for AM coupons was located; published AM studies generally report manual Archimedes measurements. | **No published robotic cycle time or success rate found.** | Trapped bubbles, wetting, suspension-wire contact, temperature, evaporation, open porosity, drying, and droplets on the balance cause failures. | **Moderate.** Feasible with a dedicated air/liquid balance, fixed basket, wetting protocol, drip tray, and automated drying—not by freehand robot motion alone. |
| **3. Solid specimens — load tensile coupons** | Universal test frames automate control and data acquisition, but no peer-reviewed flexible robot-loading system for AM ASTM E8 sub-size coupons with measured success was located. | **No published success rate or loading cycle found.** | Grip alignment, extensometer attachment, specimen identification, fractured-half retrieval, and pinch/crush hazards are unresolved. | **Conditional.** Arm can place light coupons into open self-centering grips; fixture actuation and alignment sensing must be provided by the test frame. |
| **4. Charge preparation — weigh powders/pieces** | **AlloyBot**, Selvaraj/Boonpetch 2026 preprint: robot, pellet dispensers, wire cutters, balance, and reusable copper crucibles (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 4-7, boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 13-18). **Jiang et al. 2023**: dual-arm biomimetic spatula/balance dispensing (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 2-3, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 3-4). **A-Lab** uses an automatic Quantos dispenser balance (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 7-7). | AlloyBot: approximately one alloy h⁻¹ in steady state, <0.5 h typical weighing, better than 1 at.% target accuracy, and measured compositions within EDX’s ±1 at.% uncertainty; no overall success percentage (boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 41-45, boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 30-35). Jiang: 0.07% mean error, 0.56% SD for non-challenging solids at 200 mg, but 23.1% aggregate failure; 239–552 s for NaNO₂ robot dispenses (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10). | AlloyBot evidence is a **2026 preprint**; Jiang failures include blocked outlets, deliquescence, sticking, and balance-detection errors. Neither validates combustible Al-powder containment. | **Pieces/slugs: high. Powders: conditional.** A low-payload arm can move cups, pellets, wire and small master-alloy pieces; use enclosed gravimetric dispensing for loose Al powder. |
| **4. Charge preparation — kit and load crucible/atomizer cup** | AlloyBot robotically pours weighed elemental charges into copper crucibles and orders lower-melting elements beneath higher-melting elements (boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 18-22). | Handles alloys up to 25 cm³ and over 100 g Ti-6Al-4V; load-lock permits melting to begin within 15 min and production of 24 alloys day⁻¹, with about 45 min daily crucible cleaning (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 1-4, selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 10-13). | Not demonstrated for press-fit 6063 cups/plugs, rePOWDER loading, or aluminium-powder charges; press-fitting itself may require force tooling and dimensional verification. | **High for kitting and placement.** The arm can load 250–300 g charges and cups; use a guided arbor/pneumatic press for plugs and a separate force sensor or go/no-go gauge. |
| **5. Safety — combustible metal powder and autonomous robotics** | The SDL safety literature recommends RAMP/hierarchy-of-controls, authorization, monitoring, emergency stops, collision detection, constrained motion, human review, and near-miss reporting, but gives no metal-dust-specific NFPA/ATEX implementation (leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 33-36, leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 7-11, leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 11-13, leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 1-4). A-Lab limited campaigns to air-stable targets and operated in air rather than proving inert-powder handling (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 2-3, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 1-2). | **No published success/incident rate for robots handling open combustible Al powder found. No peer-reviewed validation against NFPA 484/660 or ATEX found.** | NFPA 660/484 and the adopted fire/electrical codes require a project-specific combustible-dust hazard analysis; relevant engineering issues include ignition-capable electrical/mechanical equipment, bonding/grounding, dust-tight containment, housekeeping, ventilation/collection, explosion protection or inerting, and safe isolation. Exact obligations depend on dust explosibility data, quantity, occupancy, and authority having jurisdiction. | **Do not expose an ordinary PiPER/Raspberry Pi system to classified open-powder space without AHJ-approved design.** Prefer sealed grounded containers and a negatively contained or inert glovebox/isolator with external actuators; locate nonrated electronics outside. |
| **5. Safety — published incidents and autonomous-lab practice** | Leong et al. call for systematic near-miss reporting and note that SDL safety evidence remains immature (leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 33-36, leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 54-57). | **No peer-reviewed incident report involving an autonomous metal-powder lab was located.** Absence of reports is not evidence of safety. | Public descriptions rarely provide hazardous-area classification, dust Kst/Pmax/MIE/MEC values, cleaning validation, or ignition-source assessments. | Implement human authorization for open-powder transitions, interlocked ventilation/inerting, O₂ and pressure monitoring, spill/fire response, and remote shutdown before autonomous operation. |
| **6. Labour/time evidence — powder and alloy-development loops** | McCalla 2023 reviewed semi-automated solid-state powder workflows; A-Lab and AlloyBot provide campaign-level throughput; Von Rohr identifies preparation and characterization as persistent bottlenecks (mccalla2023semiautomatedexperimentsto pages 3-4, selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 1-4, rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 4-5). | Traditional solid-state synthesis: about 5–10 samples per researcher over three days; conventional Rietveld-quality XRD about 1 h sample⁻¹. A-Lab: 355 experiments and 41 of 58 targets synthesized in 17 days, 71% target success (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 2-3, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 4-5). AlloyBot: one alloy h⁻¹ with <1 h daily maintenance target. | **No published time-and-motion or person-hour breakdown was located for atomization followed by collection, six-fraction sieving, splitting, jarring, O/N/H sampling, SEM preparation, and flow testing.** The lab’s 10–15 hands-on h run⁻¹ estimate therefore remains plausible but externally unvalidated. | First priority should be direct timing: timestamp every container transition and weigh operation for 10–20 runs, separating hands-on, unattended, cleaning, rework, and safety/PPE time. |
| **7. Overall PiPER deployment judgment** | Existing systems show that low-payload robots are effective chiefly as sample couriers between purpose-built modules: EMSBot for stubs, A-Lab for vessels, and RASI for mounted specimens (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 6-8, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 7-8, moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 4-4). | Demonstrated modules span 5 s electrostatic deposition, 20–45 min automated SEM-EDS, up to 150 metallographic slices day⁻¹, and approximately one automatically weighed/melted alloy h⁻¹ (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 2-3, giunto2025harnessingautomatedsemeds pages 4-6, moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 2-2, boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 41-45). | Published systems rarely report recovery, cross-contamination, cleaning effectiveness, or long-run manipulation success—the metrics most important for FLAIME. | **Best near-term scope:** sealed-container logistics, weighing, identity/label verification, SEM-stub handling, instrument tending, and coupon transport. **Use dedicated industrial modules:** sieve-stack lifting, pressing, cutting, mounting, polishing force, tensile gripping, dust containment, and any operation in a classified combustible-dust zone. |


*Table: Step-by-step evidence map for automating a powder-metallurgy and AM alloy-development loop, including measured results, explicit publication gaps, and suitability for BYU’s 1.5 kg PiPER arm. Feasibility ratings distinguish lightweight robotic tending from operations requiring contained or industrial process equipment.*

---

### (1) Post-Atomization Powder Workup

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that describes a robotic or automated system for the full post-atomization workup chain—powder collection, loading sieve stacks, six-fraction classification, riffling/splitting, mass balance, jarring, labelling, or sealing O/N/H aliquots—with measured throughput, success rate, recovery, or cross-contamination control between alloys.** This represents a significant gap in the literature. Von Rohr (2024) notes that "automated grinding, sieving, and pelletizing" have "partially available commercial solutions" but that "these systems may require adaptation for the strictly controlled, inert conditions needed in autonomous materials laboratories" (rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 5-6). The closest relevant systems are mass-balance and container-transport operations demonstrated by the A-Lab and AlloyBot (discussed under charge preparation), which validate that robot-to-balance transfer of powders and solids is technically mature (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 4-7, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 7-7).

**PiPER feasibility:** The arm can serve as a lightweight courier for capped containers, individual sieve pans, and jars. However, a loaded six-sieve stack with 250–300 g powder and collection pans approaches or exceeds the 1.5 kg payload. Sieve loading/unloading, splitting, and O/N/H sample sealing (crimping) each require purpose-built fixtures or tools.

---

### (2) Powder Characterization Sample Preparation

**SEM stub preparation.** The EMSBot system (Milsted et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00116a) is the state of the art, using a modified Creality Ender3 Pro 3D printer with a vacuum-pickup robot and electrostatic deposition to disperse powder onto carbon-tape-mounted SEM stubs. It operates at "10 kV, 10 mA, and a 5-second hold time" and demonstrated "more uniform dispersion and greater particle separation" than manual preparation, with reduced agglomeration (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 2-3, milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 5-6). It retries stub pickup up to three times before requesting human intervention (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 3-5). No aggregate throughput or quantitative success rate was reported. The system is designed for integration with autonomous laboratory workflows via a "documented API, GUI, Python backend" (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 6-8). **Caution:** The electrostatic deposition method has not been validated for combustible aluminium powder, and open high-voltage dispersion near Al fines would require a formal ignition-risk assessment.

**Automated SEM-EDS analysis.** The AutoEMX framework (Giunto et al. 2025 preprint, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7837297/v1; published 2026 in Nature Communications, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x) provides fully automated particle localization, EDS spot selection, spectral fitting, filtering, and unsupervised k-means clustering for phase-resolved compositional analysis. It "typically acquires about 100 spectra" per sample "in 20–45 minutes" and "processes tens of samples per day" (giunto2025harnessingautomatedsemeds pages 4-6, giunto2026accuratesemedsquantification pages 3-5). Validated across 74 powder samples and 38 elements (nitrogen to bismuth), it "consistently estimates compositions within 5–10% of their expected values" and requires only "one experimental standard per element" (giunto2025harnessingautomatedsemeds pages 1-4, giunto2026accuratesemedsquantification pages 14-15).

**Laser diffraction, flowability, and apparent/tap density.** No peer-reviewed robotic end-to-end workflow was found for any of these tests. Published powder-flowability studies compare standardized Hall/Carney funnels and rheometers but do not describe autonomous sample loading, cleaning, or recovery (rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 5-6). These tests remain predominantly manual.

---

### (3) Solid-Specimen Steps

**Robotic metallography.** The most advanced published system is RASI (Robot-Assisted Automated Serial-Sectioning and Imaging), developed at BAM (Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung und -prüfung). It uses a "UR5e robotic arm with parallel grippers and a wrist camera, a modified Qpol250 BOT grinding/polishing unit, an etching station, an optical microscope, and a control workstation" (moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 3-4). RASI achieves "up to 150 slices per specimen per day" in "largely unattended, continuous 24/7 operation," with "XY resolution approaching 225 nm" and z-spacing "as fine as approximately 170 nm" for specimen volumes up to "approximately 15 × 15 × 15 mm³" (moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 4-4, moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 2-2). The system uses spray-based on-demand etching consuming "approximately 1–4 mL of etchant per slice, compared with roughly 60–200 mL for immersion baths" (moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 3-3). Demonstrated applications include AM 316L stainless steel melt pools, sintered steel porosity, and cast iron graphite (moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 1-2). RASI was first commissioned in 2021 and uses a UR5e (5 kg payload, ±0.03 mm repeatability) with a Python interface (lemiasheuski2023developmentofan pages 7-10). The Čermák et al. 2024 paper in *Practical Metallography* (DOI: 10.1515/pm-2024-0055, unobtainable) also addresses robotic metallographic sample preparation for precision and safety, but was not accessible for review.

**Automated hardness testing.** Commercial hardness testers with automated XY stages, autofocus, and indent recognition exist, but no peer-reviewed paper was found describing a robot-loaded hardness-testing loop for AM alloy development campaigns with measured loading success rate or cycle time.

**Archimedes density.** No peer-reviewed robotic Archimedes density workflow was located. Published AM studies universally report manual density measurements.

**Tensile specimen loading.** No peer-reviewed flexible robotic loading system for ASTM E8 sub-size tensile bars with measured success was located. Collins (2026) notes that "automated robots must be capable of handling arbitrary and widely varying complex geometries" and identifies multi-fingered, pneumatic, electro-adhesive, and soft grippers as solvable engineering problems (collins2026additivemanufacturingenabled pages 12-13).

**Part removal from build plates and sectioning.** These steps involve cutting forces, coolant, and fixturing well beyond a benchtop arm's capabilities. No alloy-development-loop paper with general robotic success metrics was located.

**PiPER feasibility:** The arm can shuttle standardized metallographic pucks and small coupons between stations but cannot supply polishing force, cutting force, or pressing force. The grinder/polisher, saw, and mounting press must operate independently.

---

### (4) Charge Preparation

**AlloyBot** (Selvaraj, Boonpetch et al. 2026, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9761885/v1; **preprint**) is the most directly relevant system. It combines "a six-axis robotic arm mounted on a horizontal seventh axis, an automatic weighing module, and an automatic arc-melting module" with 12 element channels (expandable to 24) using paired pellet dispensers and wire feeders for coarse and fine mass control (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 4-7, boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 13-18). Stated performance targets are "one alloy per hour (>150 alloys per week)" with delivery "within three hours of a request" and "less than one hour of daily human maintenance" (boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 8-13, selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 1-4). Compositional accuracy is "better than 1 at.%" with demonstrated agreement for Ti-6Al-4V, a refractory HEA, and a metallic glass (boonpetch2026alloybotsynthesisof pages 41-45). The system handles volumes up to 25 cm³ (>100 g Ti-6Al-4V) at approximately $100/5 cm³ driven primarily by feedstock cost (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 1-4). No aggregate synthesis success rate was reported.

**Biomimetic solid dispensing** (Jiang et al. 2023, DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00075c, peer-reviewed) used a dual-arm ABB YuMi robot with interchangeable 3D-printed spatulas, an analytical balance, and fuzzy-logic closed-loop control. For non-challenging solids at 200 mg, "the dual-arm robot achieved an average dispensing error of 0.07% (standard deviation 0.56%)" versus −0.41% for Quantos (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10). However, the aggregate failure rate across all 13 tested solids was 23.1% for the robot, 26.9% for Quantos, and 26.5% for Chemspeed (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11). Dispensing times were substantially longer: "552, 517, 381, and 239 seconds at 1000, 500, 200, and 20 mg targets" for the robot vs. 40–285 s for Quantos (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10).

**A-Lab** (Szymanski et al. 2023, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w, peer-reviewed, Nature) uses "a Mitsubishi robot arm" and "an automatic Quantos dispenser balance" for precursor powder dosing, followed by mixing "with ethanol and ten 5-mm ZrO₂ balls for 9 minutes in a dual asymmetric centrifuge" and transfer into alumina crucibles (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 7-7). Over "17 days of continuous operation," 41 of 58 targets were synthesized, a 71% success rate (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 2-3, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 4-5).

**PiPER feasibility for charge prep:** The arm can move cups, pellets, wire segments, and small master-alloy pieces well within 1.5 kg. For loose aluminium powder, an enclosed gravimetric dispenser (not freehand pouring) is essential for both accuracy and safety.

---

### (5) Safety: Combustible Metal Powders and Autonomous Robotics

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that specifically addresses NFPA 484 (now NFPA 660), ATEX/IECEx, or other combustible-dust standards as applied to autonomous robotic systems handling open aluminium or other combustible metal powders.** This is a critical gap.

The most relevant SDL safety publication is Leong et al. (2024, DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28, **preprint**), which recommends the "RAMP process—recognizing hazards, assessing risks, minimizing risks, and preparing for emergencies—and the hierarchy of controls" (leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 1-4). It advocates "multimodal sensing for early detection of violent bubbling, excessive heat generation, and rapid pressure buildup," constrained motion planning, emergency stops, human-in-the-loop authorization, and systematic near-miss reporting (leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 33-36, leong2025steeringtowardssafe pages 7-11). However, this paper does not mention NFPA, ATEX, combustible dust classification, dust-tight enclosures, bonding/grounding, inerting, or explosion protection.

The A-Lab deliberately restricted its campaigns to air-stable oxide and phosphate targets and operated in open air—not under inert atmosphere (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 2-3, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 1-2). AlloyBot operates under high-purity argon in its arc-melting chamber with a load-lock (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 1-4), but the safety rationale is metallurgical (oxidation prevention) rather than explosion prevention, and the weighing module appears to operate in air.

**What NFPA 660 (formerly 484) requires in general terms** (based on the standard itself, not from a peer-reviewed paper): a combustible-dust hazard analysis for the specific material; classification of electrical equipment in areas where ignitable concentrations may exist; bonding and grounding of all conductive equipment handling powder; dust-tight enclosures or ventilation/collection for dust-generating operations; housekeeping to prevent accumulation; and explosion protection (venting, suppression, or inerting) for enclosed volumes exceeding minimum explosive concentration. Standard consumer-grade electronics, including Raspberry Pi boards and unrated motor drives, are not rated for classified areas. **No published incident report involving an autonomous metal-powder laboratory was identified**, but absence of reports is not evidence of safety.

---

### (6) Time-Per-Sample and Person-Hour Breakdowns

**No published time-and-motion study or person-hour breakdown was found for the specific atomization-to-characterization workflow described in the FLAIME program** (ultrasonic atomization → collection → six-fraction sieving → splitting → jarring → O/N/H sampling → SEM stubs → flowability → printing → density/hardness/metallography/tensile testing). The lab's estimate of 10–15 person-hours per atomizer run therefore remains externally unvalidated.

The closest published comparisons come from adjacent workflows. McCalla (2023, DOI: 10.1021/acsengineeringau.3c00037, peer-reviewed) reports that traditional solid-state powder synthesis yields "approximately 5–10 samples per researcher over three days" and identifies "structural characterization" (XRD at ~1 hour/sample) as "the dominant throughput bottleneck" (mccalla2023semiautomatedexperimentsto pages 3-4). Von Rohr (2024, DOI: 10.2533/chimia.2024.855, peer-reviewed) identifies both sample preparation and characterization as persistent bottlenecks and states: "if analysis remains human-operated, it can remain the principal bottleneck" (rohr2024thechanginglandscape pages 4-5). AlloyBot reduces synthesis labor to "less than one hour of daily human maintenance" for ~24 alloys/day throughput (selvaraj2026alloybotondemandsynthesis pages 1-4).

These comparisons support the intuition that post-run powder workup and characterization preparation—not the atomization run itself—dominate hands-on time.

---

### (7) Feasibility Assessment for the PiPER Arm (1.5 kg Payload, ~15 N, Parallel Gripper, Raspberry Pi Cameras)

The evidence from published autonomous-lab implementations consistently shows that low-payload collaborative robots are most effective as **sample couriers between purpose-built processing modules**, rather than as general-purpose manipulators replacing industrial equipment. The A-Lab uses UR5e arms (5 kg payload) exclusively for crucible and labware transport between stations (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 7-8, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 8-12). RASI similarly uses a UR5e to shuttle specimens between a grinder/polisher, etching station, and microscope (moschetti2025robot‐assistedautomatedserial‐sectioning pages 3-4). EMSBot uses a modified 3D printer for the same courier function (milsted2025automatedelectronmicroscopy pages 2-3).

**Steps realistically within reach of the PiPER:**
- Sealed-container logistics: moving capped jars, vials, SEM-stub trays, and metallographic pucks between stations
- Weighing operations: placing cups on balances, triggering tare/read cycles
- Identity verification: reading AprilTags, barcodes, and labels with wrist camera
- SEM stub exchange: picking/placing lightweight stubs from trays to SEM-compatible holders
- Instrument tending: loading coupons into hardness tester nests, automated saw fixtures, or other instruments with self-clamping mechanisms
- Simple coupon transport for tensile bars and density specimens

**Steps requiring industrial or dedicated equipment (beyond the PiPER):**
- Sieve-stack assembly/disassembly with loaded powder (weight, clamping force)
- Press-fitting 6063 cup plugs (>>15 N, typically tonnes)
- Part removal from LPBF build plates (cutting forces)
- Compression/hot mounting (kN forces, 150–180°C)
- Grinding and polishing (sustained contact force, abrasive environment)
- Operations in classified combustible-dust areas (the PiPER and Raspberry Pi are not rated for such environments)

---

### Summary of Publication Status

The AlloyBot preprint (Selvaraj et al. 2026, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9761885/v1) and the Giunto et al. 2025 preprint (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7837297/v1) are **preprints** that have not completed peer review; the latter was subsequently published in *Nature Communications* in 2026 (giunto2026accuratesemedsquantification pages 8-14). The Leong et al. safety perspective (DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28) is also a **preprint**. The Collins 2026 paper (DOI: 10.1557/s43577-026-01078-y) is a peer-reviewed perspective/roadmap paper that presents an aspirational framework rather than demonstrated hardware results (collins2026additivemanufacturingenabled pages 1-2, collins2026additivemanufacturingenabled pages 10-12). All other principal sources cited (Szymanski et al. 2023 in *Nature*, Milsted et al. 2025 in *Digital Discovery*, Jiang et al. 2023 in *Digital Discovery*, Lemiasheuski et al. 2023 and Moschetti et al. 2025 in *Practical Metallography* and *Advanced Engineering Materials*, McCalla 2023 in *ACS Engineering Au*, and Von Rohr 2024 in *Chimia*) are peer-reviewed.

---

### (1) Post-Atomization Powder Workup

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that describes a robotic or automated system for the full post-atomization workup chain—powder collection, loading sieve stacks, six-fraction classification, riffling/splitting, mass balance, jarring, labelling, or sealing O/N/H aliquots—with measured throughput, success rate, recovery, or cross-contamination control between alloys.** This represents a significant gap in the literature. Von Rohr (2024) notes that "automated grinding, sieving, and pelletizing" have "partially available commercial solutions" but that "these systems may require adaptation for the strictly controlled, inert conditions needed in autonomous materials laboratories" (pqac-00000062). The closest relevant systems are mass-balance and container-transport operations demonstrated by the A-Lab and AlloyBot (discussed under charge preparation), which validate that robot-to-balance transfer of powders and solids is technically mature (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000026).

**PiPER feasibility:** The arm can serve as a lightweight courier for capped containers, individual sieve pans, and jars. However, a loaded six-sieve stack with 250–300 g powder and collection pans approaches or exceeds the 1.5 kg payload. Sieve loading/unloading, splitting, and O/N/H sample sealing (crimping) each require purpose-built fixtures or tools.

---

### (2) Powder Characterization Sample Preparation

**SEM stub preparation.** The EMSBot system (Milsted et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00116a) is the state of the art, using a modified Creality Ender3 Pro 3D printer with a vacuum-pickup robot and electrostatic deposition to disperse powder onto carbon-tape-mounted SEM stubs. It operates at "10 kV, 10 mA, and a 5-second hold time" and demonstrated "more uniform dispersion and greater particle separation" than manual preparation, with reduced agglomeration (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). It retries stub pickup up to three times before requesting human intervention (pqac-00000001). No aggregate throughput or quantitative success rate was reported. The system is designed for integration with autonomous laboratory workflows via a "documented API, GUI, Python backend" (pqac-00000000). **Caution:** The electrostatic deposition method has not been validated for combustible aluminium powder, and open high-voltage dispersion near Al fines would require a formal ignition-risk assessment.

**Automated SEM-EDS analysis.** The AutoEMX framework (Giunto et al. 2025 preprint, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7837297/v1; published 2026 in Nature Communications, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76633-x) provides fully automated particle localization, EDS spot selection, spectral fitting, filtering, and unsupervised k-means clustering for phase-resolved compositional analysis. It "typically acquires about 100 spectra" per sample "in 20–45 minutes" and "processes tens of samples per day" (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000050). Validated across 74 powder samples and 38 elements (nitrogen to bismuth), it "consistently estimates compositions within 5–10% of their expected values" and requires only "one experimental standard per element" (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

**Laser diffraction, flowability, and apparent/tap density.** No peer-reviewed robotic end-to-end workflow was found for any of these tests. Published powder-flowability studies compare standardized Hall/Carney funnels and rheometers but do not describe autonomous sample loading, cleaning, or recovery (pqac-00000062). These tests remain predominantly manual.

---

### (3) Solid-Specimen Steps

**Robotic metallography.** The most advanced published system is RASI (Robot-Assisted Automated Serial-Sectioning and Imaging), developed at BAM (Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung und -prüfung). It uses a "UR5e robotic arm with parallel grippers and a wrist camera, a modified Qpol250 BOT grinding/polishing unit, an etching station, an optical microscope, and a control workstation" (pqac-00000017). RASI achieves "up to 150 slices per specimen per day" in "largely unattended, continuous 24/7 operation," with "XY resolution approaching 225 nm" and z-spacing "as fine as approximately 170 nm" for specimen volumes up to "approximately 15 × 15 × 15 mm³" (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). The system uses spray-based on-demand etching consuming "approximately 1–4 mL of etchant per slice, compared with roughly 60–200 mL for immersion baths" (pqac-00000020). Demonstrated applications include AM 316L stainless steel melt pools, sintered steel porosity, and cast iron graphite (pqac-00000013). RASI was first commissioned in 2021 and uses a UR5e (5 kg payload, ±0.03 mm repeatability) with a Python interface (pqac-00000018). The Čermák et al. 2024 paper in *Practical Metallography* (DOI: 10.1515/pm-2024-0055, unobtainable) also addresses robotic metallographic sample preparation for precision and safety, but was not accessible for review.

**Automated hardness testing.** Commercial hardness testers with automated XY stages, autofocus, and indent recognition exist, but no peer-reviewed paper was found describing a robot-loaded hardness-testing loop for AM alloy development campaigns with measured loading success rate or cycle time.

**Archimedes density.** No peer-reviewed robotic Archimedes density workflow was located. Published AM studies universally report manual density measurements.

**Tensile specimen loading.** No peer-reviewed flexible robotic loading system for ASTM E8 sub-size tensile bars with measured success was located. Collins (2026) notes that "automated robots must be capable of handling arbitrary and widely varying complex geometries" and identifies multi-fingered, pneumatic, electro-adhesive, and soft grippers as solvable engineering problems (pqac-00000060).

**Part removal from build plates and sectioning.** These steps involve cutting forces, coolant, and fixturing well beyond a benchtop arm's capabilities. No alloy-development-loop paper with general robotic success metrics was located.

**PiPER feasibility:** The arm can shuttle standardized metallographic pucks and small coupons between stations but cannot supply polishing force, cutting force, or pressing force. The grinder/polisher, saw, and mounting press must operate independently.

---

### (4) Charge Preparation

**AlloyBot** (Selvaraj, Boonpetch et al. 2026, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9761885/v1; **preprint**) is the most directly relevant system. It combines "a six-axis robotic arm mounted on a horizontal seventh axis, an automatic weighing module, and an automatic arc-melting module" with 12 element channels (expandable to 24) using paired pellet dispensers and wire feeders for coarse and fine mass control (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). Stated performance targets are "one alloy per hour (>150 alloys per week)" with delivery "within three hours of a request" and "less than one hour of daily human maintenance" (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). Compositional accuracy is "better than 1 at.%" with demonstrated agreement for Ti-6Al-4V, a refractory HEA, and a metallic glass (pqac-00000010). The system handles volumes up to 25 cm³ (>100 g Ti-6Al-4V) at approximately $100/5 cm³ driven primarily by feedstock cost (pqac-00000009). No aggregate synthesis success rate was reported.

**Biomimetic solid dispensing** (Jiang et al. 2023, DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00075c, peer-reviewed) used a dual-arm ABB YuMi robot with interchangeable 3D-printed spatulas, an analytical balance, and fuzzy-logic closed-loop control. For non-challenging solids at 200 mg, "the dual-arm robot achieved an average dispensing error of 0.07% (standard deviation 0.56%)" versus −0.41% for Quantos (pqac-00000043). However, the aggregate failure rate across all 13 tested solids was 23.1% for the robot, 26.9% for Quantos, and 26.5% for Chemspeed (pqac-00000039). Dispensing times were substantially longer: "552, 517, 381, and 239 seconds at 1000, 500, 200, and 20 mg targets" for the robot vs. 40–285 s for Quantos (pqac-00000043).

**A-Lab** (Szymanski et al. 2023, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w, peer-reviewed, Nature) uses "a Mitsubishi robot arm" and "an automatic Quantos dispenser balance" for precursor powder dosing, followed by mixing "with ethanol and ten 5-mm ZrO₂ balls for 9 minutes in a dual asymmetric centrifuge" and transfer into alumina crucibles (pqac-00000026). Over "17 days of continuous operation," 41 of 58 targets were synthesized, a 71% success rate (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000025).

**PiPER feasibility for charge prep:** The arm can move cups, pellets, wire segments, and small master-alloy pieces well within 1.5 kg. For loose aluminium powder, an enclosed gravimetric dispenser (not freehand pouring) is essential for both accuracy and safety.

---

### (5) Safety: Combustible Metal Powders and Autonomous Robotics

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that specifically addresses NFPA 484 (now NFPA 660), ATEX/IECEx, or other combustible-dust standards as applied to autonomous robotic systems handling open aluminium or other combustible metal powders.** This is a critical gap.

The most relevant SDL safety publication is Leong et al. (2024, DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28, **preprint**), which recommends the "RAMP process—recognizing hazards, assessing risks, minimizing risks, and preparing for emergencies—and the hierarchy of controls" (pqac-00000032). It advocates "multimodal sensing for early detection of violent bubbling, excessive heat generation, and rapid pressure buildup," constrained motion planning, emergency stops, human-in-the-loop authorization, and systematic near-miss reporting (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). However, this paper does not mention NFPA, ATEX, combustible dust classification, dust-tight enclosures, bonding/grounding, inerting, or explosion protection.

The A-Lab deliberately restricted its campaigns to air-stable oxide and phosphate targets and operated in open air—not under inert atmosphere (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). AlloyBot operates under high-purity argon in its arc-melting chamber with a load-lock (pqac-00000009), but the safety rationale is metallurgical (oxidation prevention) rather than explosion prevention, and the weighing module appears to operate in air.

**What NFPA 660 (formerly 484) requires in general terms** (based on the standard itself, not from a peer-reviewed paper): a combustible-dust hazard analysis for the specific material; classification of electrical equipment in areas where ignitable concentrations may exist; bonding and grounding of all conductive equipment handling powder; dust-tight enclosures or ventilation/collection for dust-generating operations; housekeeping to prevent accumulation; and explosion protection (venting, suppression, or inerting) for enclosed volumes exceeding minimum explosive concentration. Standard consumer-grade electronics, including Raspberry Pi boards and unrated motor drives, are not rated for classified areas. **No published incident report involving an autonomous metal-powder laboratory was identified**, but absence of reports is not evidence of safety.

---

### (6) Time-Per-Sample and Person-Hour Breakdowns

**No published time-and-motion study or person-hour breakdown was found for the specific atomization-to-characterization workflow described in the FLAIME program** (ultrasonic atomization → collection → six-fraction sieving → splitting → jarring → O/N/H sampling → SEM stubs → flowability → printing → density/hardness/metallography/tensile testing). The lab's estimate of 10–15 person-hours per atomizer run therefore remains externally unvalidated.

The closest published comparisons come from adjacent workflows. McCalla (2023, DOI: 10.1021/acsengineeringau.3c00037, peer-reviewed) reports that traditional solid-state powder synthesis yields "approximately 5–10 samples per researcher over three days" and identifies "structural characterization" (XRD at ~1 hour/sample) as "the dominant throughput bottleneck" (pqac-00000035). Von Rohr (2024, DOI: 10.2533/chimia.2024.855, peer-reviewed) identifies both sample preparation and characterization as persistent bottlenecks and states: "if analysis remains human-operated, it can remain the principal bottleneck" (pqac-00000063). AlloyBot reduces synthesis labor to "less than one hour of daily human maintenance" for ~24 alloys/day throughput (pqac-00000036).

These comparisons support the intuition that post-run powder workup and characterization preparation—not the atomization run itself—dominate hands-on time.

---

### (7) Feasibility Assessment for the PiPER Arm (1.5 kg Payload, ~15 N, Parallel Gripper, Raspberry Pi Cameras)

The evidence from published autonomous-lab implementations consistently shows that low-payload collaborative robots are most effective as **sample couriers between purpose-built processing modules**, rather than as general-purpose manipulators replacing industrial equipment. The A-Lab uses UR5e arms (5 kg payload) exclusively for crucible and labware transport between stations (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027). RASI similarly uses a UR5e to shuttle specimens between a grinder/polisher, etching station, and microscope (pqac-00000017). EMSBot uses a modified 3D printer for the same courier function (pqac-00000002).

**Steps realistically within reach of the PiPER:**
- Sealed-container logistics: moving capped jars, vials, SEM-stub trays, and metallographic pucks between stations
- Weighing operations: placing cups on balances, triggering tare/read cycles
- Identity verification: reading AprilTags, barcodes, and labels with wrist camera
- SEM stub exchange: picking/placing lightweight stubs from trays to SEM-compatible holders
- Instrument tending: loading coupons into hardness tester nests, automated saw fixtures, or other instruments with self-clamping mechanisms
- Simple coupon transport for tensile bars and density specimens

**Steps requiring industrial or dedicated equipment (beyond the PiPER):**
- Sieve-stack assembly/disassembly with loaded powder (weight, clamping force)
- Press-fitting 6063 cup plugs (>>15 N, typically tonnes)
- Part removal from LPBF build plates (cutting forces)
- Compression/hot mounting (kN forces, 150–180°C)
- Grinding and polishing (sustained contact force, abrasive environment)
- Operations in classified combustible-dust areas (the PiPER and Raspberry Pi are not rated for such environments)

---

### Summary of Publication Status

The AlloyBot preprint (Selvaraj et al. 2026, DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-9761885/v1) and the Giunto et al. 2025 preprint (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7837297/v1) are **preprints** that have not completed peer review; the latter was subsequently published in *Nature Communications* in 2026 (pqac-00000046). The Leong et al. safety perspective (DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-2qx28) is also a **preprint**. The Collins 2026 paper (DOI: 10.1557/s43577-026-01078-y) is a peer-reviewed perspective/roadmap paper that presents an aspirational framework rather than demonstrated hardware results (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059). All other principal sources cited (Szymanski et al. 2023 in *Nature*, Milsted et al. 2025 in *Digital Discovery*, Jiang et al. 2023 in *Digital Discovery*, Lemiasheuski et al. 2023 and Moschetti et al. 2025 in *Practical Metallography* and *Advanced Engineering Materials*, McCalla 2023 in *ACS Engineering Au*, and Von Rohr 2024 in *Chimia*) are peer-reviewed.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated powder-transfer and sample-preparation workflow for PXRD, not post-atomization workup for oxygen analysis. Samples were crystallized, dried, fitted with Kapton-taped septa caps and magnetic stir bars, stirred for two minutes, then inverted cap-down in a shaker plate. Shaking transferred powdered material directly onto the taped caps, eliminating a separate post-grinding inversion step. Transfer was quantitatively assessed by weighing caps before and after shaking at 2, 4, 8, and 16 minutes. The reported average transfer was approximately 10% after two minutes, with little average improvement through 16 minutes; the text estimates that approximately 100 mg starting material was needed to obtain 10 mg for good PXRD data. Failure modes included powder compaction against vial walls, incomplete transfer when vials were tipped, powder falling back into vials during cap reorientation, and possible loss of adhered powder during prolonged agitation. Robotic operations used a dual-arm YuMi to move vials, unscrew caps, and place caps into a preparation plate. A printed holder enabled regripping, and gripper force was reduced from 20 N to 10 N to prevent finger deformation and breakage. No specific procedures, throughput, cycle times, success rates, or failure modes are provided for sieving, splitting, mass-balance accounting, jarring, labelling, sealing for oxygen analysis, or atomized powders.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes EMSBot as a solvent-free, modular automated system for depositing inorganic powder samples onto SEM stubs or TEM grids within self-driving laboratory (SDL) workflows. It combines a modified Creality Ender3 Pro 3D printer with a control panel, custom 3D-printed trays, a sample exposition station, and a vacuum handling robot. For SEM preparation, carbon-tape-mounted SEM stubs are picked up by vacuum, positioned near an electrode, and exposed to powder in a secured sample container. Deposition is electrostatic: a high-voltage power supply energizes the SEM electrode wire connected to a sharp SEM needle, while induced charge attracts powder particles onto the carbon tape. The reported SEM operating conditions are 10 kV, 10 mA, and a 5-second hold time. EMSBot can be controlled remotely through a Python backend and socket requests for SDL integration, or through a browser-based webpage interface. The excerpt also indicates that operating conditions can affect particle-size dispersion and may enable preferential deposition of smaller particles. However, these pages do not report the system’s throughput or success rate; those metrics would need to be obtained from later experimental-results sections of the article.

contexts.context: The excerpt introduces EMSBot as an automated robot for preparing powder samples for SEM and TEM within self-driving laboratories. Its purpose is to replace difficult-to-reproduce manual handling of tiny quantities of powder and sample holders, improving consistency and integration with existing SDL hardware and software. The system uses a modular, user-friendly design based on a modified 3D printer: the original nozzle is replaced by a custom handling robot that holds needles for picking up SEM stubs and TEM grids. Its printer bed is replaced with a 5 mm-thick polypropylene bed for electrical insulation, and custom 3D-printed trays hold SEM stubs and TEM grids. A removable SEM-stub tray allows clean stubs to be exchanged easily. For conventional SEM preparation, powder is drop-cast onto a stub covered with carbon or copper tape, followed by removal of excess material with an air blower or gentle tapping; the article states that EMSBot produces more consistent and higher-quality powder dispersions than this manual approach. contexts.context: AlloyBot is an automated bulk-alloy synthesis platform integrating robotic charge preparation, precision weighing, arc melting, and optional suction casting. Its robot module uses a UR10 six-axis arm with a custom pick-and-place end effector mounted on a horizontal rail that functions as a seventh axis, allowing movement among the weighing and melting modules. The weighing module dispenses pure elemental feedstock into reusable copper crucibles, which serve as both transfer vessels and melting containers. It currently has 12 pellet-and-wire dispenser pairs and can prepare arbitrary compositions from 12 stocked elements, with possible expansion to 24 pairs. Approximately 3 mm pellets provide rapid, coarse mass delivery through rotating-disk dispensers, while 0.5–1.0 mm elemental wire is advanced by pinch rollers and cut into controlled-length segments for fine mass correction. The stated compositional accuracy is well below 1 at.%. After weighing, the robot transfers the crucible to a load-lock and then into the arc-melting chamber, where automated transfer, repeated melting, flipping, and remelting promote homogenization. AlloyBotMaster coordinates the equipment, while AlloyBotBrain records process metadata. The excerpt does not report numerical throughput or synthesis success rate; it only indicates that the design targets improved throughput and reproducibility.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes AlloyBot as an integrated robotic system that automatically weighs elemental feedstock and transfers it to an automated arc-melting stage. Its weighing module uses paired pellet dispensers and wire feeders, with 12 element channels in the current configuration and possible expansion to 24. Pellets provide efficient coarse mass delivery, while short wire segments enable fine composition corrections. For each requested alloy composition and volume, the robot places a stainless-steel weighing cup on an analytical balance, dispenses the required pellets and wire until the target mass is reached, removes the cup, and finally pours each elemental charge into a clean copper crucible. Elements are stacked according to melting temperature, with lower-melting elements nearer the crucible bottom. The crucible is then transferred to the arc-melting module, which melts, repeatedly processes for homogenization, and can suction-cast the alloy into rods. Resolution depends on alloy volume, feedstock geometry, and molar density: a 3 mm pellet may contribute about 2.5 at.% in a 1 cm³ alloy, whereas a 2 mm × 1 mm wire segment contributes about 0.16 at.%. contexts.context: AlloyBot is an integrated, automated system for on-demand synthesis of bulk alloys. It combines a six-axis robotic arm mounted on a horizontal seventh axis, an automatic weighing module, and an automatic arc-melting module, coordinated by an industrial supervisory computer (AlloyBotMaster) and a data/metadata computer (AlloyBotBrain). The system can prepare alloy volumes up to 25 cm3, equivalent to more than 100 g of Ti-6Al-4V, and is currently configured for arbitrary compositions using 12 stocked metallic elements, with expansion to 24 dispenser pairs planned. The weighing module uses separate pellet and wire dispensers for each element: pellets provide coarse, economical dosing, while accurately cut wire segments provide fine mass adjustment through closed-loop balance feedback. The robot places cups on the scale, pours weighed components into a reusable copper crucible, and orders low-melting elements below higher-melting elements for charging. A weighing cycle takes less than one hour. Stated dispensing accuracy is better than 1 at.%; for a 2 mm by 1 mm wire segment, the nominal contribution is approximately 0.16 at.% in a 1 cm3 alloy and below 0.01 at.% in a 25 cm3 alloy. contexts.context: The excerpt describes AlloyBot as an automated arc-melting platform that combines robotic charge handling, mobile copper crucibles, a load-lock chamber, automatic crucible transfer, multi-electrode arc melting, and dedicated continuous gettering. Robotically prepared feedstock is stacked into crucibles at a weighing module; the crucible and charge are then handled as one unit and transferred into the load-lock without exposing the melting chamber to air. A forklift-like transfer mechanism moves the crucible through a gate valve into the melting chamber and inserts it into the hearth cavity. The stated throughput is 24 alloys per day using 25 clean crucibles, with one contaminated crucible set aside per hour and approximately 45 minutes of daily manual cleaning. The load-lock design reduces atmosphere-restoration time so melting can begin in under 15 minutes. contexts.context: The excerpt describes AlloyBot as an automated arc-melting architecture intended to reduce manual intervention and improve reproducibility. Its melting module replaces the conventional manually swept single electrode with four independently powered electrodes arranged symmetrically around the chamber and angled toward the copper crucible hearth. The converging arcs heat the charge simultaneously, allowing feedstock to melt, merge into a liquid droplet, and solidify into an alloy button without electrode scanning. Electrode currents may be varied to promote magnetohydrodynamic mixing, and the electrodes use actuated longitudinal and transverse motions for working-distance adjustment and clearance. Its functions include mechanical polishing, etching, and optical imaging, and its architecture is centered on a six-axis collaborative robot. Fresh, uncontaminated etchant is applied for every slice, improving reproducibility and avoiding performance drift; the approach also permits use of unstable etchants without retaining waste in a bath. contexts.context: This excerpt characterizes BAM’s robot-assisted automated serial-sectioning and imaging (RASI) system as a robotic serial-sectioning and imaging workflow designed for three-dimensional metallographic investigations. Its robotic arm and three-point kinematic sample coupling provide highly repeatable positioning between imaging cycles, with lateral variation below the micrometer scale and rotational variation below one degree. Residual alignment errors are corrected semi-automatically in Fiji using SIFT registration, followed by cropping to the common area of interest. The system combines approximately 300+ μm XY resolution with z-direction resolution as fine as 0.17 μm and can process volumes up to approximately 15 × 15 × 15 mm³. Demonstrated analytical outcomes include quantitative characterization of grain, pore, and precipitate morphology, size, and spatial distribution; grain-boundary and network connectivity, including twin boundaries; and geometric measures such as aspect ratio, Feret diameter, and tortuosity. In a sintered steel specimen, RASI revealed true pore interconnectivity that cannot be established from conventional 2D metallography. The supplied pages do not report cycle times or describe the degree of automated grinding and polishing, so those requested details require other sections of the article.

It provides automated sample preparation, heating, and powder X-ray diffraction characterization. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the A-Lab as an autonomous platform for solid-state synthesis of inorganic powders. It combines ab initio phase-stability data from the Materials Project and Google DeepMind, literature-trained machine-learning models, active learning, robotics, and automated X-ray diffraction analysis. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the A-Lab as a bespoke, fully automated platform for solid-state synthesis and powder X-ray characterization. It contains an automated precursor-preparation station with a Mitsubishi robot arm, an automatic Quantos dispenser balance, a pipettor, four box furnaces with custom door actuators, a product-handling station, a powder X-ray diffractometer, and UR5e collaborative robot arms that move samples and labware. Operators manually load plastic vials, zirconia milling balls, crucibles, and precursor bottles containing 50–100 g of powders at the beginning of a campaign. contexts.context: Jiang et al. evaluated a dual-arm biomimetic robotic solid-dispensing platform against Quantos and Chemspeed automated gravimetric powder-dosing systems. The study tested 13 solids, including inorganic, organic, abrasive, coarse, and moisture-sensitive materials, across three target masses. Accuracy was assessed using percentage weighing error, defined as (dispensed mass minus target mass) divided by target mass times 100; failed dispenses counted as 100% error. The biomimetic robot performed better on average than the two commercial benchmark systems for non-challenging solids at the 200 mg target scale. However, when challenging solids were included, some failed to dispense, and the average error became much higher and approximately comparable across all three platforms. Quantos and Chemspeed periodically produced large over-dispensing errors when their dosing heads or cartridges failed to close, potentially because of partial blockages. Coarse sand was particularly incompatible with Quantos dispensing heads, while sugar generally dispensed accurately on Chemspeed but occasionally produced severe over-dispenses. The excerpt provides no throughput rate, cycle time, or detailed Kadokawa robotic powder-weighing results; those systems cannot be characterized from this passage.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Jiang et al.’s autonomous biomimetic solid-dispensing workflow using a seven-degree-of-freedom dual-arm robot, an analytical balance with a sliding door, a receiving vial, a hopper, a funnel, and interchangeable custom 3-D-printed spatulas. The robot opens the balance, places and weighs the vial, positions and mixes the hopper contents to break agglomerates, scoops material, and dispenses it through a funnel by tilting and shaking. A closed-loop fuzzy-logic controller adjusts shaking frequency and spatula tilt according to the remaining weight error and particle granularity. Spatula selection is weight-dependent: large for amounts above 0.8 g, medium for approximately 0.1–0.8 g, and small for amounts below 0.1 g. The system accommodates large particles, mixed particle sizes, and abrasive materials. After each dispensing episode, the weight is updated and the process stops when the error is within tolerance. Excess material can be returned to the hopper, and a reset operation returns all material when over-dispensing exceeds a preset threshold. contexts.context: Jiang et al. evaluated a biomimetic dual-arm robotic solid-dispensing system against a Quantos dispenser and a Chemspeed platform using thirteen solids and multiple target weights. For non-challenging solids at a 200 mg target, the dual-arm robot achieved an average dispensing error of 0.07% (standard deviation 0.56%), comparable to Quantos at −0.41% (1.80%) and better than Chemspeed at −2.23% (12.39%). Across all solids, average errors were −22.85% for the robot, −23.39% for Quantos, and −17.39% for Chemspeed, reflecting failures and difficult materials rather than routine precision. The robot was substantially slower: for sodium nitrite with 2 mg tolerance, dispensing times were 552, 517, 381, and 239 seconds at 1000, 500, 200, and 20 mg targets, respectively; Quantos required 40, 33, 31, and 285 seconds, while Chemspeed required 134, 132, 109, and 62 seconds. Robot delays arose from manipulating multiple tools and repeating dispensing after over-dosing. Failure causes included blocked funnels or spatula outlets, hygroscopic/deliquescent materials sticking to surfaces, abrasive solids, and robot balance-detection errors. contexts.context: Giunto et al. describe AutoEMX as a fully automated, high-throughput SEM-EDS workflow for compositional analysis of powders. After sample loading, the user supplies SEM-stage stub coordinates and the elements present; candidate phase compositions can optionally be provided. The system detects and subdivides carbon tape into frames, segments and localizes particles, automatically selects EDS spot positions, acquires spectra, fits them, and quantifies elemental mass fractions. Automated filtering removes measurements affected by analytical-total errors, absorption, insufficient background counts, substrate contamination, or poor spectral fitting. The retained compositions are then analyzed with machine learning, including k-means clustering, to determine phase number and composition and to assign candidate single phases or two-phase mixtures with confidence scores. The framework combines a particle-based peak-to-background quantification method, automated acquisition/filtering, and ML analysis, requiring only one experimental standard per element. The excerpt reports benchmarking on 74 single-phase powder samples, with 2,483 spectra retained after filtering. Accuracy is evaluated using relative deviation (RDEV) for individual measurements and cluster centroids, plus absolute deviation (ADEV) for centroid compositions; figures specifically assess 5% and 10% relative-error and 1 and 2 at% absolute-error bands, although the excerpt does not provide the associated percentages. AutoEMX also resolves minor inclusions, mixtures, and deviations that XRD-only analysis may miss.

contexts.context: Giunto et al. describe AutoEMX as a locally running Python package that automates SEM-EDS powder characterization on instruments with a Python API. The workflow requires only the sample-stub position and a list of potentially present elements; optional expected phase compositions can support candidate-based phase assignment. AutoEMX locates the carbon tape using the navigation camera, divides it into a grid, randomly samples fields, and uses 15 kV backscattered-electron imaging to segment particles by intensity thresholding. Particles larger than 4 µm² are retained, recentered, and magnified. Up to five randomly selected spot spectra are collected per particle, at least 1 µm from particle edges and from one another, to reduce substrate contamination and capture compositional heterogeneity. Acquisition targets 50,000 total counts per spot, normally taking 6–15 seconds, with a 30-second maximum. The system collects up to 100 spectra or stops when particles are exhausted, requiring approximately 20–45 minutes per sample. Spectral fitting, quantification, and machine-learning analysis were performed offline in this study, although real-time analysis and autonomous termination based on confident phase-cluster assignment are supported. The excerpt gives methodological safeguards for accuracy, including calibrated peak models and background/absorption treatment, but it does not provide numerical accuracy metrics. It also refers to AutoEMX, not explicitly “AutoEMXSp.”

contexts.context: Giunto et al. describe AutoEMXSp, a fully automated SEM-EDS workflow for phase-resolved compositional characterization of as-deposited powder samples. The system combines automated EDS spectrum acquisition and quantification, data filtering, and unsupervised machine learning to identify compositional groups and resolve multiphase, minor, or intermixed phases, while reporting confidence scores. Its quantification strategy uses peak-to-background measurements to reduce geometry-related mass and absorption artifacts caused by irregular powder particles. A key practical feature is that it requires only one experimental standard per element, including for light elements that are conventionally difficult to quantify in powders. The workflow is designed for operator-free, high-throughput operation and is reported to process tens of samples per day across a broad chemical space. The authors validate it on 74 powder samples containing elements from nitrogen through bismuth. AutoEMXSp typically achieves atomic-fraction measurements within 5–10% relative deviation from expected compositions and resolves minor or intermixed phases with high confidence. The stated goal is integration with autonomous or self-driving laboratories, where large sample numbers and low-uncertainty compositional data are needed for machine-learning-guided materials discovery.

contexts.context: Giunto et al. describe AutoEMXSp, a Python-based workflow for automated, high-throughput SEM-EDS compositional analysis of as-deposited powder samples, demonstrated on a cost-effective desktop SEM-EDS system. The workflow integrates four stages: autonomous detection of the carbon-tape region and grid-based search, particle segmentation and localization, automated selection of multiple EDS measurement spots, quantitative spectral fitting, filtering of unreliable measurements, and machine-learning analysis—specifically k-means clustering—to identify phase populations and compositions. The required user inputs are the sample’s microscope-stage position and the set of elements expected; candidate phase compositions can optionally be supplied for comparison and identification. Particles larger than approximately 2 µm are favored to reduce mass effects, and up to five spectra may be acquired per particle at positions away from edges to limit substrate contamination. The reported operating scale is typically about 100 spectra per sample, each collected to 50,000 counts, requiring approximately 20–45 minutes. The excerpt reports atomic-fraction relative deviations generally below 5–10% for tested samples spanning elements from nitrogen to bismuth, while also indicating high-confidence resolution of minor or intermixed phases. Improved background, absorption, and geometry corrections support quantification of light elements such as N, O, and F.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes AutoEMX as an automated SEM-EDS workflow designed for high-throughput powder characterization. It uses experimental, standard-based P/B quantification with stopping-power corrections, allowing one standard per element to be applied across samples with widely different average atomic numbers. Standards acquisition and calibration are automated, with only an initial measurement needed to establish a reference set for future analyses on the same instrument. The workflow automatically filters spectra affected by substrate contamination, X-ray absorption, poor fitting, geometry-related artifacts, or analytical totals that deviate substantially from 100 wt%. The retained measurements are grouped using unsupervised k-means clustering to identify distinct phases, quantify uncertainties, and match measured compositions to candidate phases with confidence scores. Broad or ambiguous clusters can be interpreted as two-phase mixtures using NNLS, or decomposed with NMF when candidate phases are unavailable. Reported accuracy is generally better than 5–10% relative deviation from expected composition values. The benchmark included 74 single-phase powders, spanning oxides, phosphates, and silicates, 38 elements, and atomic numbers 7–83. The excerpt does not provide a numerical spectra-per-hour, sample-per-hour, or other explicit throughput value; it supports the high-throughput claim through automation of acquisition, calibration, filtering, clustering, phase identification, and reporting.
